ecolongr

Community ecology analyses with an aim to complement Vegan for large datasets based on long tables. The priorities are memory economy first and efficiency second.

ecolongr computes diversity, distances, transformations and ordinations from a table with one row per sample and taxon, without the zeros. The taxa × samples matrix that vegan needs is never built. Results are tested against vegan and have vegan’s classes. metaMDS(), adonis2(), betadisper(), hclust() and cmdscale() give vegan’s results on a distance, and scores(), summary(), plot(), biplot(), envfit() and procrustes() work on an ordination.

The functions are documented one by one on the package website, with examples that run on the table bundled in the package.

Why

Amplicon data has millions of ASVs and thousands of samples, and almost every cell is zero. vegan needs the dense matrix: 500,000 ASVs × 20,000 samples is about 80 GB of doubles. ecolongr works on the non-zero rows only, in the form the data is delivered in. For a table of that size, el_vegdist() took 25 seconds and 2.4 GB with 12 threads, of which 1.6 GB is the result itself.

Bray-Curtis distances on synthetic tables, one run each; the memory is the peak of the whole R process:

table ecolongr vegan
500 samples, 41,090 taxa 0.4 s, 270 MB 47 s, 530 MB
2,000 samples, 158,708 taxa 3.1 s, 390 MB more than 33 min, at least 4.1 GB
3,000 samples, 235,740 taxa 5.7 s, 480 MB not run

ecolongr ran on one thread, as vegan does. The slow vegan run on the 2,000-sample table was stopped by hand, so its memory is what it held at that point. The 3,000-sample table was run only with ecolongr: scaling the 500-sample time with the square of the samples and the number of taxa, vegan would need about 2.5 hours. The timings of vegan varied by a factor of two between runs on a machine under load. The Bioconductor package mia calls vegan::vegdist() on the dense matrix, so it takes as long as vegan does.

Status

Early development, version 0.1.1. The functions are tested against vegan, but names and arguments may still change. Design, scope and open questions are in DESIGN.md.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("biodiversitydata-se/ecolongr", build_vignettes = TRUE, dependencies = TRUE)

build_vignettes = TRUE builds the vignettes, which needs pandoc; leave it out without pandoc, and read them on the package website instead.

The package contains C++ code (Rcpp, with OpenMP if your compiler has it), so it needs a C++ compiler. It uses duckplyr for the lazy table operations.

Reading a table

The input is a table with a sample, a taxon and a quantity column, with zeros left out. ecolongr works on lazy tables from duckplyr. A lazy table is a query that DuckDB runs only when a result is needed, so reading, filtering and joining the table never loads it into R. Parquet files suit this best, because DuckDB reads only the columns and row groups a query needs. nf-core/ampliseq 3.0.0 and later write such a table to summary_tables/ampliseq.counts.parquet.

library(duckplyr)
library(ecolongr)

counts <- read_parquet_duckdb("summary_tables/ampliseq.counts.parquet", prudence = "stingy") |>
  transmute(sample, taxon = asv_id, quant = count)

prudence = "stingy" makes duckplyr stop with an error where it would otherwise silently copy the whole table into R. Text files work too, and keep memory low in the same way:

counts <- read_csv_duckdb(
  "counts.tsv.gz",
  options = list(delim = "\t", header = TRUE),
  prudence = "stingy"
)

DuckDB parses a text file again for every query. To pay that cost once, write the table to Parquet with compute_parquet(counts, "counts.parquet") and read that file in the later steps. A data frame in R is accepted as well, but it is already in memory. ecolongr does not attach duckplyr: attach it yourself, as above, to use its verbs on the table.

The default column names are sample, taxon and quant, and every function has arguments with the same names to point at other columns. The package bundles a small table, 347 samples of a 16S time series from the Baltic Sea, that the examples in the function help pages use:

counts <- read_csv_duckdb(
  system.file("extdata", "lmo_free_living.tsv.gz", package = "ecolongr"),
  options = list(delim = "\t", header = TRUE), prudence = "stingy"
)
metadata <- read.delim(system.file("extdata", "lmo_free_living_samples.tsv", package = "ecolongr"))

A table without zeros cannot show a sample that has no rows at all. Pass samples = metadata$sample to el_vegdist() and el_rda() to include such samples, as vegan does with a zero row, and to set the order of the result to that of the metadata. This matters before envfit(), adonis2() or procrustes(), which pair rows by position.

Data from asvoccur

asvoccur reads datasets downloaded from the Swedish ASV portal. It returns a sparse matrix, which Matrix::summary() turns into a long table:

loaded <- asvoccur::load_data("path/to/datasets")
merged <- asvoccur::merge_data(loaded)

triplets <- Matrix::summary(merged$counts)
counts <- data.frame(
  sample = colnames(merged$counts)[triplets$j],
  taxon = rownames(merged$counts)[triplets$i],
  quant = triplets$x
)

merged$events has the sample metadata, with eventID matching the sample names. asvoccur does not yet have a long-table form of its own; asvoccur#1 proposes one.

Alpha diversity

Richness and diversity indices of each sample (el_specnumber(), el_diversity()), richness at a common depth (el_rarefy(), el_drarefy(), el_rrarefy()) and the frequency table that richness estimators need (el_frequency_counts()). They correspond to vegan::specnumber(), diversity(), rarefy(), drarefy() and rrarefy().

The first two return one number per sample, as a vector named by sample:

richness <- el_specnumber(counts)
shannon <- el_diversity(counts, "shannon")      # or "simpson", "invsimpson"; `base` sets the logarithm

diversity <- tibble(sample = names(shannon), shannon = shannon, richness = richness[sample]) |>
  left_join(metadata, by = "sample")

Richness grows with the number of reads, so compare samples at a common depth. el_rarefy() gives the richness each sample is expected to have in a subsample of depth reads, which is exact and needs no random numbers. el_rrarefy() draws one random subsample, as vegan::rrarefy() does, and returns a table; use it when you need the subsampled table itself.

depth <- counts |>
  summarise(reads = sum(quant, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) |>
  summarise(depth = min(reads)) |>
  pull(depth)

expected_richness <- el_rarefy(counts, depth)

set.seed(1)
subsample <- el_rrarefy(counts, depth)

Estimators of the total richness, including the taxa not seen, such as breakaway, fit a model to the number of taxa seen once, twice and so on. el_frequency_counts() computes that table for all samples in one lazy step, and the fits then run on small tables, one per sample, in parallel if you like:

frequencies <- counts |> el_frequency_counts() |> as.data.frame()

# breakaway reads one table per sample, sorted by count.
per_sample <- frequencies |>
  arrange(sample, count) |>
  split(~ sample) |>
  purrr::map(\(d) select(d, count, n_taxa))

estimates <- per_sample |>
  purrr::map(purrr::in_parallel(\(d) breakaway::breakaway(d)))   # after mirai::daemons(4)

breakaway’s estimates depend strongly on its cutoff argument, and tables without singletons, such as DADA2 output, need breakaway::breakaway_nof1(). ecolongr does not reimplement these estimators.

Beta diversity and ordination

The steps from a table to a distance matrix and an ordination:

  1. Filter the table with duckplyr verbs, which stay lazy.
  2. Standardise it with el_decostand() (total, hellinger, log, pa or rclr), also lazy.
  3. Compute distances with el_vegdist(): bray, jaccard, euclidean, manhattan, canberra, aitchison or robust.aitchison. The result is a dist, and vegan takes over.
  4. Or compute the principal components with el_rda(), which returns the first k axes as an rda object.
# 1. ASVs present in at least 20% of the samples, and samples with at least 5,000 reads.
n_samples <- counts |> summarise(n = n_distinct(sample)) |> pull(n)

common <- counts |>
  summarise(prevalence = n_distinct(sample), .by = taxon) |>
  filter(prevalence >= 0.2 * n_samples) |>
  select(taxon)

deep <- counts |>
  summarise(depth = sum(quant, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) |>
  filter(depth >= 5000) |>
  select(sample)

filtered <- counts |>
  semi_join(common, by = "taxon") |>
  semi_join(deep, by = "sample")

# 2 and 3. Relative abundances and Bray-Curtis distances.
# Nothing is read into R until el_vegdist().
# `samples` sets the order of d to that of the metadata and includes samples without counts.
d <- filtered |>
  el_decostand("total") |>
  el_vegdist("bray", samples = metadata$sample)

# d is a dist object: use vegan on it.
ordination <- vegan::metaMDS(d)
vegan::adonis2(d ~ treatment, data = metadata)
vegan::envfit(ordination, metadata[, c("temperature", "salinity")], na.rm = TRUE)

metaMDS() on a dist has no species scores; giving it the matrix would, but needs the dense table.

A PCA of the centred log-ratio (clr) of the counts needs a pseudocount, because the logarithm of zero is not defined. "inverse_depth" uses one over the sample’s total count, and a numeric vector named by sample sets it freely. "inverse_depth" takes the totals of the table it is given, which after the filters above are smaller than the libraries, by different amounts in different samples. Pass the depths from before filtering by name instead:

depth <- counts |>
  summarise(total = sum(quant, na.rm = TRUE), .by = sample) |>
  as.data.frame()
pseudocount <- purrr::set_names(1 / depth$total, depth$sample)

# 4. A PCA of the clr, first five axes.
pca <- filtered |>
  el_rda(k = 5, transform = "clr", pseudocount = pseudocount, samples = metadata$sample)

summary(pca)
plot(pca)

# Axis labels with the percentage of the total variance: divide by tot.chi, not by sum(eigenvals).
percent <- 100 * vegan::eigenvals(pca)[1:2] / pca$tot.chi
plot(
  vegan::scores(pca, display = "sites", choices = 1:2),
  xlab = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", percent[1]), ylab = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", percent[2])
)
vegan::envfit(pca, metadata[, c("temperature", "salinity")], choices = 1:2, na.rm = TRUE)

The prevalence filter matters for clr: on a 60,633-ASV time series with 99% zeros, the seasonal cycle showed poorly in a clr PCA until ASVs present in fewer than 20% of the samples were removed. duckplyr translates few R functions, so filter(.by = ) is not available (use summarise(.by = ) and a join, as above), sum() needs na.rm = TRUE, and a scalar with names, such as the result of quantile(), must go through unname().

clr is not a method of el_decostand(), because it makes every cell non-zero, which a table without zeros cannot hold. It is computed from the raw counts inside the two functions that use it: el_vegdist(method = "aitchison") is the Euclidean distance between clr-transformed samples, which is the Aitchison distance, and el_rda(transform = "clr") is a PCA of the clr, whose sample distances with all axes are the same Aitchison distances.

A longer walk-through, from the published time series to seasonal ordinations and alpha diversity, is in the vignette seasonal-ordination, or vignette("seasonal-ordination", package = "ecolongr").

Where results differ from vegan

Distances, standardisations, diversity indices and expected richness equal vegan’s to about 1e-10, and PCA scores to about 1e-8 (1e-6 with the iterative solver on large tables). The tests compare every function and option with vegan on varespec, BCI and a synthetic community. The differences that matter:

  • el_rrarefy() is random and does not give vegan’s subsample for the same seed; it draws from the same distribution.
  • el_decostand("rclr") leaves zeros absent, which vegan’s completed rclr does not; el_vegdist(method = "robust.aitchison") and el_rda(transform = "rclr") run the same completion as vegan.
  • metaMDS() on the dist has no species scores.
  • el_rda() returns the first k axes only, so predict() and fitted() give an error. Divide an eigenvalue by pca$tot.chi, never by the sum of the kept eigenvalues, to get the share of the whole variance.
  • el_rarefy() has no se, and a sample with no non-zero row is absent from the alpha diversity results, where vegan gives it a row of zeros.

All of them, with the reasons, are in the vignette differences-from-vegan.

Memory and speed

el_vegdist() runs the lazy query in DuckDB, writes it to a temporary Parquet file sorted by taxon, and reads it back in batches of whole taxa. A compiled kernel adds up the pairs into one vector in the order of a dist object. The memory has three parts:

  • the result, one number per pair of samples, which grows with the square of the number of samples;
  • one batch of rows;
  • the memory DuckDB uses for the sort, which memory_limit caps (250 MB by default).

Measured on a 24-thread desktop under load, on synthetic tables where a few taxa occur in nearly every sample:

table el_vegdist() el_rda()
5,000 samples, 11.1M rows 7 s with 12 threads (30 s with one), 1.0 GB 35 s, 1.4 GB
20,000 samples, 19.4M rows 25 s with 12 threads (148 s with one), 2.4 GB 63 s, 2.2 GB

Settings:

  • threads (option ecolongr.threads, default half the cores) sets the threads of the distance kernel. The result is identical for any number.
  • memory_limit (option ecolongr.memory_limit, default "250MB") limits the memory DuckDB uses for sorting, and it spills to disk beyond that.
  • batch_rows (default 1,000,000) is roughly how many table rows are in R at a time.

ecolongr does not change the settings of your duckplyr session. The lazy steps you write before calling it, such as el_decostand(), run there with DuckDB’s defaults (all cores, 80% of the memory). On a small machine, limit them:

duckplyr::db_exec("SET memory_limit = '1GB'")
duckplyr::db_exec("SET threads = 4")

On the 5,000-sample table this took the peak of a total plus Euclidean pipeline from 2.4 GB to 1.1 GB at a cost of 3 seconds.
